messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajiv is a 58-year-old South Asian man married with two children. He has worked as a bomb disposal technician for over three decades, but his life changed dramatically when his youngest child fell critically ill five years ago. The hospital stay was harrowing, marked by constant medical interventions and the ever-present antiseptic smell that Rajiv could not escape. The memory of those days still haunts him. Just walking past a hospital or even catching a whiff of antiseptic can instantly bring back the full weight of those memories. He recalls the sterile corridors, the beeping machines, and the faces of worried medical staff as though he were right there again. The visual imagery is vivid—images of his child hooked up to IV drips and surrounded by needles are particularly painful reminders. Rajiv’s sleep has been severely disrupted since then. Each night, he tosses and turns, unable to fall asleep because a part of him remains vigilant, waiting for something terrible to happen again. He feels as though the trauma is still unfolding around him, making it impossible to relax. This constant state of alertness exacerbates his physical reactivity; whenever he encounters a trigger, his heart races, and he breaks into a cold sweat. His negative emotions are intense, and fear is at the forefront—fear that he won’t be able to protect his child or any other child again. Rajiv has come to believe that he is weak, unable to handle such immense stress and responsibility. He is also deeply afraid that these reactions mean he’s losing his mind, which only adds to his sense of vulnerability. The triggers serve as a constant reminder of the traumatic event, and they are intertwined with his negative appraisals and heightened threat perception. Whenever he sees needles or medical equipment, it brings back full sensory reliving of those moments in the hospital. The memory is so vivid that he can hear the beeps of the machines and feel the cold floor beneath him as though he were still there. Rajiv’s fear of going crazy has only intensified this cycle. He believes his reactions to triggers are signs of a deeper psychological instability, making it harder for him to trust himself and his ability to manage such situations in the future. This belief feeds into his sense of helplessness, which in turn reinforces his threat perception. The event itself was so traumatic that even being around children now sets off these painful memories. The hospital stay and medical interventions were so intense that any reminder brings back a complete sensory experience—almost as if he is reliving it again. This makes everyday activities extremely difficult for him, especially given his occupation where the presence of medical equipment can be common. Rajiv’s job often requires him to work in environments where antiseptic smells are prevalent and where medical supplies like needles and drips are commonplace. These triggers have made his work environment a minefield of emotional discomfort, leading to frequent absences and a gradual decline in performance. Over the past few months, Rajiv has noticed that these symptoms have become more persistent, affecting not just his work but also his home life. His wife is increasingly concerned about his state and encourages him to seek help. What frightens him most is the fear of being unable to protect his family and the constant worry that he might lose control again. Rajiv’s negative appraisals have become deeply ingrained, making it hard for him to believe in any future where he can regain a sense of stability or strength. He hopes that with help, he can break free from this cycle and find a way to reconnect with his family without the constant fear overshadowing everything. His current state is a delicate balance between wanting support and fearing further weakness. Rajiv’s journey towards seeking therapy marks a step towards reclaiming control over his life, hoping for relief from the relentless loop of triggers, memories, and negative beliefs that have come to define his daily existence.
